\paragraph{Scope of claims.}
Our analyses are observational: we compare trained and reference checkpoints but do not intervene on the training process itself.
All findings are correlational associations between training status and representational structure; we cannot distinguish whether exit collapse is caused by action fine-tuning or by confounded factors (e.g., data distribution, optimization trajectory).
The cross-architecture design ($N = 2$ independent VLM-to-VLA transitions) strengthens external validity relative to single-architecture studies but remains insufficient for strong causal claims.
We use ``associated with'' rather than ``produces'' throughout to reflect this evidential status.
A visual summary of the claim-evidence structure appears in Figure~\ref{fig:claim_evidence} (Appendix~\ref{sec:claim_evidence_appendix}).

\paragraph{Synthesis.}
VLA fine-tuning is associated with two representational changes (peak-to-exit action-probe decodability drops and counterfactual sensitivity) that concentrate at the readout token (training shifts readout $R^2$ by $+0.069$ vs.\ image\_mean by $+0.015$).
L1 instruction attention is inherited from base-model pretraining (Phi-3-Vision: 32/32, Qwen2.5-VL: 13--14/16 before training).
VLA fine-tuning does not build instruction routing from scratch; downstream representations differ between trained and reference models while early-layer attention structure is preserved.

\paragraph{VLM-to-VLA vs.\ VLA-to-VLA transitions.}
Exit collapse separates cleanly by effect size: substantial ($\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.455$, all $> 0.10$) in every VLM-to-VLA trained cell, but only small fluctuations ($\Delta R^2 = 0.033$--$0.086$, all $< 0.10$) under VLA-to-VLA conditions.
Two independent VLM-to-VLA transitions (TracVLA and NORA, with distinct backbone families) converge on the same large effect, compatible with task-structure constraints of causal-decoder VLA design rather than architecture-specific artifacts.
The small $\Delta R^2$ under VLA-to-VLA conditions is consistent with the OXE-pretrained baseline having already adapted at exit layers during its initial action training on 970K episodes; LIBERO fine-tuning, operating on a model that has already adapted for action prediction, does not produce further substantial collapse.
Mid-layer probes outperform exit-layer probes for action prediction in architectures exhibiting pronounced collapse, suggesting potential efficiency gains from early-exit inference.
Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with LIBERO success rates yields a positive but non-significant trend ($\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Cross-architecture evidence rests on $N = 2$ independent VLM-to-VLA transitions; OpenVLA tests a different transition type.
All experiments use LIBERO; benchmarks with richer language grounding are needed.
We analyze only causal-decoder VLAs; flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} architectures may differ.
NORA lacks 2 of 4 suite checkpoints, and each architecture is analyzed at a single trained checkpoint (extended discussion in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).
The NLP fine-tuning control covers only the Llama-2 backbone; extending to Phi-3 and Qwen2.5 backbones would strengthen the VLA-specificity argument.
All analyses are open-loop (offline, on pre-recorded trajectories); closed-loop behavioral validation connecting representational findings to task performance is left for future work.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
We analyzed three VLA architectures across four LIBERO task suites, comparing trained and reference checkpoints.
VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning is associated with substantial $R^2$ exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.15$--$0.45$) across all tested conditions, whereas VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning and reference models show only small fluctuations ($\Delta R^2 < 0.10$).
All trained VLAs exhibit medium-to-large counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.97$), while L1 instruction attention is inherited from base-model priors.
An NLP finetuning control ($\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) further supports transition-type specificity.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

1	\paragraph{Conclusion.}
2	We analyzed three VLA architectures (OpenVLA, TracVLA, NORA) across four LIBERO task suites, comparing trained and reference checkpoints to decompose VLA fine-tuning into training-associated and inherited representational effects.
3	Two training-associated effects are consistent across two VLM-to-VLA transitions: $R^2$ exit collapse, where action-relevant information encoded at intermediate layers is selectively less decodable at exit layers (6/6 cells, sign test $p = 0.016$), and counterfactual sensitivity, where all trained models respond to instruction perturbation (Cohen's $d \geq 0.45$ across eight tested cells).
4	Exit collapse universally marks the VLM-to-VLA transition and re-emerges for spatially demanding tasks under VLA-to-VLA conditions (2/4 cells), suggesting that exit-layer reorganization scales with the representational distance between pretraining and target tasks; an NLP finetuning control on the same backbone ($\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) confirms this effect is specific to action-oriented training.
5	In contrast, L1 instruction-dominant attention is inherited from base-model pretraining: one backbone (Phi-3-Vision) saturates at 32/32 heads before any action training.
6	Metric incomparability between trained (action MSE) and reference (cosine distance) conditions precludes quantifying counterfactual amplification factors, and the task-dependent nature of VLA-to-VLA collapse (2/4 OpenVLA suites) indicates that exit reorganization is modulated by pretraining-target distance rather than being universally triggered by further fine-tuning.
7	Extending this framework to flow-matching and diffusion VLAs with cross-attention, to benchmarks with richer language grounding, and to intermediate training checkpoints are priorities for future work.

1	Vision-language-action (VLA) fine-tuning adapts pretrained vision-language or language backbones for robotic action prediction, but how this process reorganizes instruction-related representations remains poorly understood.
2	We study this question through a cross-architecture representational analysis of OpenVLA, TracVLA, and NORA across four LIBERO task suites, comparing trained checkpoints with their corresponding reference models.
